title: Exploding the Notion of “Solo Piano” in Parallel Universes
content_blocks: Parallel Universes adds one more element to be exploded: solo piano. Exploding the idea of ‘solo’ is straightforward: the very first prelude-and-fugue pair in the set adds whistling at the beginning and ending of the fugue, voice is added at the beginning of Fugue No.12, an optional additional bass line in the piano at the end of that fugue, and finally Prelude and Fugue No.13 is for two pianos.

The term ‘piano’ is far more interesting. 2025 marks the 200th anniversary of the first use of a cast iron frame in piano construction, and the use of crossed strings (the lowest strings running above some of the other strings) was developed between 1825 and 1859, when Steinway first used it on their grand pianos. These two characteristics most distinguish modern pianos from the earlier fortepianos. For the rest (felt-covered hammers that strike the strings and then bounce back away, dampers that move off the string when they are sounding and return to stop the strings when the key and/or the damper pedal is released), while there have been improvements over the 250-year history of pianos and fortepianos, how a piano worked was usually taken for granted.

This began to be questioned by composers Henry Cowell and then John Cage.  I’ve been told that Cage first started experimenting with ways to modify pianos while accompanying dance classes at UCLA in the late 1930s.  His first composition for “prepared piano” was written in 1940.  Cage’s piano preparations consisted largely of screws, bolts, and rubber stoppers placed between the strings, along with thumbtacks pushed into the hammers.  I spent more than six months experimenting with a truly wide range of materials to insert into the strings, including chopsticks, straws, golf tees, sponges, alligator clips, metal clothespins, tambourine jangles, metal pull-chains, snare drum snares, paper, Blu Tack (poster putty), pencils, and decks of cards and books, as well as the screws, bolts, and rubber erasers or wedges that Cage had used.  I also used heavy beach towels to muffle the sound.

The modified sound worlds these preparations created (which can seem familiar—reminiscent of Indonesian gamelan, Chinese temple bells and the Guqin, drum corps, a jazz quartet, and Eastern European klezmer—and yet also so “other”) motivated me to write the music. That is, I didn’t set out to create a gamelan sound; rather certain group of preparations inspired me to explore that sound world. Other sound worlds are completely different from pre-existing traditions, but are made more familiar through association with visual arts—paintings, sculptures, photographs—that served as further inspiration.

This second book represented the culmination of what I had started with the first book. The exploration of mode continues—four use newly created modes—but more use pre-existing world music modes: two use klezmer modes, two use Indonesian gamelan modes, two use the most common form of pentatonic mode, and for two pitches are so unrecognizable (because of the preparations) that the written notes are irrelevant. The last pair, written in C minor and C major, respectively, represent a return to western classical roots. The last fugue is also a culmination of the total collection of 26 preludes and fugues in that it is a five-voice triple fugue (don’t worry if you don’t know what that means—but be impressed!). Thankfully there is a second pianist involved, making that gargantuan structure feasible.

I spent more than six months experimenting with…chopsticks, straws, golf tees, sponges, alligator clips, metal clothespins, tambourine jangles, metal pull-chains, snare drum snares, paper, Blu Tack (poster putty), pencils, and decks of cards and books, as well as screws, bolts, and rubber erasers or wedges.
